title: Water Leak Sensors for Older Adults' Homes: What They Do, What They Cost
subtitle: A small leak sensor can give an early warning, as long as you know what it can and cannot do.
excerpt: A leaking water heater or a cracked washer hose can go unnoticed for a while. Here is how simple water leak sensors work, what two of them cost and where to put them.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Most water damage starts quietly. A washing machine hose cracks, a toilet supply line drips, or an old water heater begins to seep in a basement nobody visits often. By the time someone notices a soft floor or a musty smell, the repair bill can be large.

A water leak sensor is a small battery-powered device that you place on the floor where leaks tend to happen. When it detects moisture, it sounds an alarm, sends a warning to a phone, or both, depending on the model. For an older parent living alone, or a grown child who lives a few hours away, that can mean hearing about a leak sooner.

Each sensor watches for water at the spot where you put it. Depending on the model, it can sound an alarm in the room, send an alert through a phone app, or do both. Moen's detector, for example, can send alerts through its app, text, phone call or email, depending on your settings.

Many sensors connect to your home Wi-Fi, which is the wireless internet signal from your router. Some models need a small box called a hub or gateway to pass the message along, so check what comes in the box. Some models also track room temperature and humidity, which can help flag frozen pipes in winter or damp conditions that can lead to mold.

It is important to be clear about the limits. A sensor only warns you. It does not turn off the water. Stopping the flow automatically takes a separate shutoff valve, which is a different and pricier product. A sensor also only detects water right where it sits, so a leak in the next room will go unnoticed. Phone alerts depend on working Wi-Fi, a working router and a phone that someone is carrying and has turned on. If the internet goes down, app alerts can be lost.

items: A loud local alarm. If your parent does not use a smartphone, a beep they can hear in the house helps when someone is home. Check the alarm volume for the model you choose, since not every product page states it.
Who gets the alerts. App alerts can go to an adult child's phone instead of, or as well as, the parent's. Some systems also offer text, phone call or email alerts.
What is in the box. Check whether you need a hub, gateway or other base unit, and whether it is included.
Price per sensor. Packs and single units are sold differently, so divide the price by the number of sensors before comparing.
Monthly fees. We saw no monthly fee on either product page below, but could not check for optional paid plans, so ask before you buy.
Battery life. Batteries need replacing eventually, so check the stated battery life and battery type for each model.
General tip: look for an easy return policy and a way to reach support, in case the app setup gets stuck.

sections.content: Setting them up and using them well

Placement does most of the work. Good spots include under the kitchen and bathroom sinks, behind each toilet, next to the washing machine, beside the water heater and in the basement. Moen suggests a basement, washing machine or hot water tank. Follow the maker's instructions for where and how to set each sensor.

If a grown child is handling setup, it often makes sense to install the app on their phone and, if the parent is comfortable, on the parent's phone too. Agree in advance on who checks on an alert and who calls the plumber. As a general tip, a neighbor with a spare key can be a helpful backup.

Test each sensor after setup and every so often after that, using the test method in the maker's instructions, since the right method can differ by model. Confirm that the alarm sounds and that the alert reaches the right phone. Testing also shows whether Wi-Fi or batteries have quietly failed.
sections.label: Setup Tip

sections.content: Also learn where the main water shutoff valve is in the house, and make sure everyone who might respond to an alert knows too. A sensor can tell you there is a leak, but someone still has to turn off the water.

A few sensors in the right places can be a useful extra layer of warning, though they do not replace checking hoses and appliances now and then. Start with the spots most likely to leak, test the sensors from time to time, and keep a plan for who responds.

products.price: $153.68 sale price, regular price $240.00 (Moen's site, November 2026); stock not confirmed
products.blurb: Suits families who want alerts by app, text, phone call or email, depending on your settings. Moen calls it "a standalone sensor that can be placed anywhere in a home," and it also tracks temperature and humidity. That works out to roughly $51 per sensor (approximate), compared with $43.99 for one Govee unit. The page's Add to Cart button read "Checking Availability," so stock was not confirmed. The page did not give battery life or alarm volume. It states no monthly fee, but optional paid plans could not be checked.

products.name: GoveeLife Smart Water Leak Detector with Wi-Fi Gateway
products.price: $43.99, marked down from $54.99 (Govee's collection page, November 2026; the product page showed no price, so check the current price there)
products.blurb: Suits someone who wants a single sensor with a Wi-Fi gateway for one or two trouble spots. Govee's collection page, not the product page, lists it as IP67 waterproof with a 5-year battery life. These are manufacturer claims we could not confirm on the product page, so check the battery for the model you buy. The alarm volume was not confirmed. We saw no monthly fee, but optional paid plans could not be checked.
